life_summary: George Quayle Cannon was born January 11, 1827, in Liverpool, England, to parents who were converted to the Latter-day Saint faith. His family immigrated to America when he was young, settling in the growing LDS communities in the Midwest and eventually moving west with the main body of the church. Cannon developed early aptitude in languages and printing, which became crucial to his later ecclesiastical responsibilities. He married Elizabeth Hoagland, with whom he had children, and in accordance with church doctrine practiced plural marriage, ultimately taking six wives and fathering thirty-three children who became prominent citizens and leaders in Utah and beyond. Cannon's education and talent for languages made him invaluable to the church's international missionary efforts.
church_summary: Cannon was called to the apostleship on August 26, 1860, at age thirty-three, and immediately began serving in the First Presidency under four successive church presidents: Brigham Young, John Taylor, Wilford Woodruff, and Lorenzo Snow. He was the founding publisher and owner of The Juvenile Instructor magazine (1866), serving in that capacity until his death in 1901. He also served as the first general superintendent of the church's Sunday School from 1867 to 1901. Cannon held multiple significant church positions simultaneously: he was a five-time territorial delegate to the U.S. Congress (1872–1882), managing editor of the Deseret News (1867–1874), and an Oregon and California Mission President (1856–1858). He translated the Book of Mormon into Hawaiian, demonstrating his commitment to making scripture accessible to diverse peoples.
